title: When the Interior Sings
premise: Yara Ashgrove, night librarian in a city that never sleeps, catalogues silences the way others catalogue books. When a radio plays a song that was written for them and never recorded — composed by their late brother, Theo, whose death they never properly mourned — Yara begins hearing fragments of it everywhere, each one tied to an unsaid goodbye. As the family house sale closes in ten days, Yara must return to it, confront the mother who chose duty over love, and finally speak the words they've hoarded for years. The novel ends with Yara singing the song aloud in the empty house as the buyers sign downstairs, choosing to belong to themselves at last.
about_author: L. M. Ishikawa is a former night-shift archivist who wrote this debut over three years of insomniac dawns. They live near water and believe every house keeps a record of what was never said in it.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. We meet Yara shelving returned books at 3 a.m., keeping a private ledger of sentences never spoken — to Theo before his death, to their mother, to themselves. A closing notice for the Ashgrove house arrives by post. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: A Song With No Source
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. On the drive home, the radio plays a melody Yara knows was never recorded — Theo's unfinished composition, hummed once in the kitchen years ago. The DJ has no record of it. Yara starts hearing it in dripping taps and passing cars. Beat: uncanny grief cracking open routine.

chapters.title: What the Mother Kept
chapters.summary: Yara visits their mother, Odile, in the half-empty house to collect documents for the sale. Odile is brisk, efficient, erasing Theo's room first. Yara finds sheet music hidden under floorboards — the full song, finished after all. Beat: anger and longing braided together.

chapters.title: Ten Days to Empty
chapters.summary: Alternating Yara and Odile POVs. Odile's chapter-within reveals she heard Theo play it the night he died and forbade him from pursuing music; her silence since has been penance she mistakes for strength. Neither says any of this aloud. Beat: two people circling the same wound.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Marisol, an old neighbor, recalls Theo playing his song on the porch for someone he loved — a person Yara never knew existed. Jealousy and tenderness collide; Yara realizes the song wasn't only for them. Beat: the dead become larger than memory allowed.

chapters.title: Duty, Sung Backwards
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Flashback to Odile's own abandoned singing career, sacrificed for respectability, and how she demanded Theo make the same trade. She hears the melody in her sleep now too. Beat: the corruption of power wielded 'for your own good.'

chapters.title: The Person in the Song
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara tracks down Dev, Theo's partner, who has been quietly attending open houses pretending to be a buyer just to see the house again. Dev carries the last verse Theo wrote, unsent. Beat: grief shared becomes bearable; love against duty made flesh.

chapters.title: Closing Day Approaches
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Storm knocks out power; mother and child trapped together overnight among boxed lives. The song plays faintly through a battery radio neither turned on. Nearly-speaking, they retreat again. Beat: highest tension — the almost-confession that fails.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Signing morning. Yara climbs to Theo's bare room, unfolds the sheet music, and sings the whole song badly and completely, voice breaking then steadying. Odile appears in the doorway and, for the first time, harmonizes. Beat: climax — the goodbye finally said, out loud, together.

chapters.title: What Sings After
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, weeks later. The house belongs to strangers; Yara keeps the sheet music, not the guilt. They begin recording the song with Dev, and leave the ledger of unsaid things blank on purpose. Final beat: belonging chosen, not inherited — the interior sings because it is no longer full.
